newsitem.title: MEXICO: MCI, Banamex ready to take on Telmex in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: MCI, Banamex ready to take on Telmex in Mexico.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp. and Mexican financial group Banamex-Accival say their joint telephone venture Avantel is set to take on Telefonos de Mexico next month, when the Mexican phone giant loses its historic monopoly.

Avantel, a company created by the U.S.-based carrier and Mexico's largest bank, has already laid down 5,500 kilometres (3,400 miles) of fiber-optic cable in Mexico, signed up scores of corporate clients and launched an aggressive advertising campaign to coax customers from long-time provider Telmex.
"I am very bullish about what we have accomplished and what we are going to accomplish," Dan Crawford, president and chief operating officer of Avantel, said in an interview.

Crawford shows visitors a cartoon of a jogger labelled Avantel racing around a track while other would-be rivals of Telmex sit on the sidelines in their warm-up suits. The message, he says, is clear: Avantel is way ahead of everyone else in getting ready for competition.
"At this point in time ... of all the carriers that said they wanted to be involved (in the Mexican market) ... only one has met all of its commitments," Crawford said.
By the end of 1997, Avantel will have spent $600 million in capital and another $300 million in human resources, marketing and other non-capital spending, Crawford said.

At stake is a $4 billion-a-year market in long-distance alone -- a market expected to double in five years. Crawford said he expects long-distance minutes growth of at least 17 percent a year, nearly twice the U.S. rate.

Avantel aims to have 20 percent of the market within five to seven years. Officials are wary of predicting how fast they will gain market share, however, saying much depends on how the government regulates the market and if Telmex plays fair.

One early problem has been government delays in sending out ballots that allow potential customers to pre-subscribe to Avantel as their long-distance company. If customers do not choose a carrier ahead of time, they can pick a long-distance company for each individual call by dialing a prefix.
If customers do not return ballots or dial a prefix, their call will automatically go to Telmex.

"We don't think its particularly fair, but we've accepted it. Having said that, we think it's incumbent upon the government to ensure there is a strong turnout (in the pre-subscription process)," Crawford said.
He also said Telmex was using its role as a local service provider to gain advantages in its long-distance business.
"We order services from Telmex on behalf of our clients, clients who may never have seen a Telmex salesman see a long-distance salesman the next day," Crawford said.
"They'll make promises to get a circuit to them in two weeks. We had been waiting six months to get it for them. Now they are offering them a much shorter time," he said.
Crawford said new competitors will be keen to see if the government chooses a carrier other than Telmex, which is seen to maintain a heavy influence on the government.
Avantel says its long-distance rates will be on average 10 percent lower than Telmex. But officials play down the possibility of a damaging price war.
